messages.content: What is Newton's second law and how is it used?

Newton's second law of motion states that the net force acting on an object equals the product of its mass and acceleration: F = ma. This is the central equation of classical mechanics, connecting kinematics (the description of motion) to dynamics (the causes of motion). Force (F) is a vector quantity measured in Newtons (N = kg·m/s²); mass (m) is a scalar measured in kilograms; acceleration (a) is a vector measured in m/s². Because force and acceleration are vectors, the law applies component-by-component. The net force is the vector sum of all forces on the object (gravity, normal force, friction, tension, etc.) — individual forces must be added vectorially before applying F=ma. Applications: (1) Projectile motion: horizontally, F_net=0, so a_x=0 (constant velocity). Vertically, F_net=-mg (gravity), so a_y=-g (constant downward acceleration). This gives the parabolic trajectory. (2) Circular motion: centripetal acceleration a=v²/r directed toward the centre; the centripetal force (provided by tension, friction, gravity, normal force) = mv²/r. (3) Atwood machine: two masses m₁ and m₂ connected by a rope over a frictionless pulley; apply F=ma to the system: (m₁-m₂)g = (m₁+m₂)a. Momentum formulation: F = dp/dt (rate of change of momentum p=mv) — more general, applicable when mass changes (rockets, variable mass systems). The first law (inertia) and third law (action-reaction) complete the framework. Limitations: Newton's laws fail at very high velocities (special relativity) and very small scales (quantum mechanics).
What is thermodynamics and what are its four laws?

Thermodynamics is the branch of physics dealing with heat, work, temperature, and their relation to energy, entropy, and properties of matter. It emerged from the study of steam engines and was developed into a rigorous science by Carnot, Clausius, Kelvin, and Gibbs. Zeroth Law: if two systems are each in thermal equilibrium with a third, they are in thermal equilibrium with each other. This establishes temperature as a measurable property and justifies thermometers. First Law (Conservation of Energy): the internal energy U of a closed system changes according to: ΔU = Q - W, where Q is heat added to the system and W is work done by the system. Energy is conserved — it cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred or converted. A 'perpetual motion machine of the first kind' (creates energy from nothing) is impossible. Second Law: entropy S of an isolated system tends to increase (or remain constant) over time; it never spontaneously decreases. Clausius: heat spontaneously flows from hot to cold, never the reverse. Kelvin: no heat engine can convert thermal energy to work with 100% efficiency. The Carnot efficiency is the maximum possible: η = 1 - T_cold/T_hot. A 'perpetual motion machine of the second kind' (extracts useful work from a single heat source) is impossible. Third Law: as temperature approaches absolute zero (0K), the entropy of a perfect crystal approaches a constant minimum (zero for a perfect crystal). It is impossible to cool a system to absolute zero in a finite number of steps. Entropy: S = k_B ln(W), where W is the number of microstates corresponding to the macrostate (Boltzmann's equation). The second law has profound implications: the arrow of time, the impossibility of perfect engines, the tendency of systems toward disorder.
What is quantum mechanics and why is it so strange?

Quantum mechanics (QM) is the physical theory that governs the behaviour of matter and energy at the scale of atoms and subatomic particles. It replaces classical mechanics in the microscopic domain and has been tested to extraordinary precision — the most accurate physical theory ever devised. Why it is strange: (1) Wave-particle duality: quantum objects (electrons, photons) exhibit both wave-like properties (interference, diffraction) and particle-like properties (localised detection events). The double-slit experiment: a single electron sent through two slits produces an interference pattern on a detector — as if it passed through both slits simultaneously. When you detect which slit the electron passes through, the interference pattern disappears. (2) Superposition: a quantum system can exist in a superposition of multiple states simultaneously. The wavefunction Ψ(x,t) encodes all information about the system — |Ψ|² gives the probability density of finding the particle at position x. The system only 'collapses' to a definite state upon measurement. Schrödinger's cat: a thought experiment showing the absurdity of applying superposition to macroscopic objects. (3) Uncertainty principle (Heisenberg): Δx · Δp ≥ ℏ/2. Position and momentum cannot be simultaneously known to arbitrary precision. This is not a limitation of our measurement tools but a fundamental feature of nature. Similarly ΔE · Δt ≥ ℏ/2. (4) Quantum entanglement: two particles can be correlated in a way that measuring one instantaneously affects the other, regardless of separation. Not faster-than-light communication (cannot send information), but violates local hidden variable theories (Bell's theorem, confirmed by Aspect's experiments). (5) Quantisation: energy, angular momentum, and other quantities can only take discrete values.
What is special relativity and what are its key predictions?

Special relativity was developed by Albert Einstein in 1905 (On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies). It is based on two postulates: (1) The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames. (2) The speed of light in vacuum c ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s is the same in all inertial frames, regardless of the motion of the source or observer. From these two postulates flow radical predictions: Time dilation: moving clocks run slower relative to stationary observers. Δt' = γ·Δt where γ = 1/√(1-v²/c²) ≥ 1. At v=0.87c, γ≈2: a moving clock ticks at half the rate. Confirmed by: muon experiments (muons created in upper atmosphere survive to sea level only because time dilation extends their lifetime), atomic clocks on aircraft (Hafele-Keating experiment, 1971), GPS corrections (GPS satellites must correct for both special and general relativistic effects). Length contraction: moving objects are shortened along the direction of motion. L' = L/γ. At v=0.87c, γ≈2: a moving rod is half its rest length. Relativity of simultaneity: events simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another — this is the most counterintuitive result. Mass-energy equivalence: E = mc² — mass and energy are equivalent and interconvertible. A stationary particle has rest energy mc²; a moving particle has total energy γmc². This explains why nuclear reactions release enormous energy: small amounts of mass convert to vast energy. No object with mass can reach c (would require infinite energy at v→c). The Lorentz transformation replaces the Galilean transformation of classical mechanics for converting between inertial frames.
What is electromagnetism and explain Maxwell's equations?

Electromagnetism is the unified theory of electric and magnetic phenomena, developed by James Clerk Maxwell in the 1860s, building on the experimental work of Faraday, Ampère, Coulomb, and Gauss. Maxwell's four equations describe all classical electromagnetic phenomena: (1) Gauss's Law for Electricity: ∇·E = ρ/ε₀. The divergence of the electric field equals the charge density divided by the permittivity of free space. Electric field lines begin and end on charges; electric charge is the source of the electric field. In integral form: the total electric flux through any closed surface equals the enclosed charge divided by ε₀ (Gauss's law). (2) Gauss's Law for Magnetism: ∇·B = 0. The divergence of the magnetic field is zero — there are no magnetic monopoles; magnetic field lines form closed loops. (3) Faraday's Law: ∇×E = -∂B/∂t. A changing magnetic flux induces a circulating electric field. This is the basis of electrical generators and induction motors. (4) Ampère-Maxwell Law: ∇×B = μ₀J + μ₀ε₀∂E/∂t. Electric current AND changing electric fields produce magnetic fields. Maxwell added the second term (displacement current) — crucial for consistency and for predicting electromagnetic waves. From these equations, Maxwell derived that E and B fields can propagate as waves in vacuum with speed c = 1/√(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3×10⁸ m/s — matching the known speed of light, leading Maxwell to conclude that light is an electromagnetic wave. The electromagnetic spectrum: radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, gamma rays — all are electromagnetic waves differing only in frequency. Maxwell's equations are Lorentz invariant — they obey special relativity — unlike Newton's laws.
What is the photoelectric effect and what does it tell us about light?

The photoelectric effect is the emission of electrons from a material when light is incident on it. Observed experimentally by Hertz (1887) and studied by Lenard (1902), it produced results that defied classical electromagnetic wave theory. Classical predictions vs. observations: Classical: the energy of emitted electrons should depend on the intensity (amplitude) of the light — brighter light should produce faster electrons. Observation: intensity affects the number of electrons, not their energy. Classical: with very dim light, electrons should take time to absorb enough energy. Observation: emission is instantaneous even for very dim light. Classical: any frequency of light should eventually emit electrons if bright enough. Observation: there is a threshold frequency below which no electrons are emitted regardless of intensity. Einstein's 1905 explanation (for which he won the 1921 Nobel Prize): light consists of discrete packets of energy called photons. Each photon has energy E = hf (h = Planck's constant, f = frequency). For an electron to be emitted, a single photon must give the electron enough energy to overcome the work function φ (binding energy of the electron in the material). K.E._{max} = hf - φ. This explains all observations: (1) Threshold frequency: hf < φ means no emission regardless of intensity. (2) Intensity determines photon number, hence electron count — not electron energy. (3) Instantaneous emission: each photon-electron interaction is immediate. The photoelectric effect was key evidence for the quantisation of light (wave-particle duality) and the reality of photons, previously introduced by Planck in 1900 to explain blackbody radiation. Applications: solar panels, light detectors, photomultiplier tubes, digital cameras (charge-coupled devices).
What is nuclear physics and explain nuclear fission and fusion?

Nuclear physics studies the structure and behaviour of atomic nuclei. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons (collectively nucleons) held together by the strong nuclear force — a short-range (~1 fm = 10⁻¹⁵ m) but enormously powerful force that overcomes the electromagnetic repulsion between protons. Binding energy: the energy required to completely separate a nucleus into its constituent nucleons. Binding energy per nucleon peaks at iron-56 (~8.8 MeV/nucleon) — the most tightly bound nucleus. Elements lighter than Fe release energy by fusion; elements heavier than Fe release energy by fission. Fission: a heavy nucleus (e.g., U-235) splits into two lighter daughter nuclei when struck by a neutron, releasing 2-3 neutrons and enormous energy (~200 MeV per fission event). The released neutrons can trigger further fissions — chain reaction. Controlled chain reaction: nuclear reactor (moderator slows neutrons for efficient U-235 capture; control rods absorb neutrons to regulate criticality). Uncontrolled chain reaction: atomic bomb. Products include radioactive isotopes — nuclear waste management is a major challenge. Fusion: two light nuclei combine to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. In the sun: the proton-proton chain fuses hydrogen to helium; per nucleon, fusion releases more energy than fission. E = Δm·c² (mass defect converts to energy). Requires extremely high temperature (~10⁷ K for the sun; ~10⁸ K in reactors — to overcome Coulomb barrier via quantum tunnelling and thermal energy). Fusion energy: ITER (France) and NIF (USA) are pursuing fusion power. In December 2022, NIF achieved ignition — more fusion energy out than laser energy in — a milestone. Fusion advantages: fuel (deuterium from seawater) is virtually unlimited; no long-lived radioactive waste; no chain reaction risk.
What is wave-particle duality and the de Broglie hypothesis?

Wave-particle duality is the fundamental quantum mechanical property that all matter and radiation exhibit both wave-like and particle-like characteristics depending on the type of interaction or measurement. It represents a departure from classical thinking, where waves (light) and particles (matter) are distinct. Photons: light exhibits wave behaviour (interference, diffraction, polarisation) and particle behaviour (photoelectric effect, Compton scattering — photon-electron collisions where photon wavelength increases, consistent with a particle imparting momentum). De Broglie hypothesis (1924): if light (classically a wave) can behave as particles (photons), then perhaps matter (classically particles) can exhibit wave behaviour. Louis de Broglie proposed that any particle with momentum p has an associated wavelength: λ = h/p where h is Planck's constant. For a particle of mass m and velocity v: λ = h/(mv). De Broglie's hypothesis was confirmed experimentally by Davisson and Germer (1927): electrons were scattered by a nickel crystal and produced a diffraction pattern — conclusive evidence of electron wave behaviour. For everyday objects: a tennis ball (m=0.06kg, v=30m/s) has λ = 6.626×10⁻³⁴/(0.06×30) ≈ 3.7×10⁻³⁴ m — unmeasurably small; this is why quantum effects are unobservable in everyday life. For electrons: at typical atomic velocities, λ is on the order of atomic spacings (0.1-1 Å) — exactly why electrons can diffract from crystal lattices. Applications: (1) Electron microscopy: electron wavelengths shorter than visible light allow resolution of nanometre-scale structures (SEMs, TEMs). (2) Neutron scattering: structural analysis of materials. (3) Quantum mechanics: Schrödinger's wave equation describes the evolution of the de Broglie waves.
What is general relativity and how does it describe gravity?

General relativity (GR, Einstein 1915) is the modern theory of gravity, replacing Newton's instantaneous action-at-a-distance gravitational force with a geometric description of curved spacetime. The core idea: mass and energy curve spacetime; objects in curved spacetime follow the straightest possible paths (geodesics) — what we perceive as gravity is simply the natural motion in curved spacetime. Einstein field equations: G_μν + Λg_μν = (8πG/c⁴)T_μν. G_μν is the Einstein tensor (describes spacetime curvature — encodes how spacetime is curved by the matter-energy within it); T_μν is the stress-energy tensor (describes matter and energy distribution); Λ is the cosmological constant (dark energy). Key predictions confirmed experimentally: (1) Light deflection: light follows geodesics in curved spacetime, so massive objects bend light paths. The sun deflects starlight by 1.75 arcseconds — confirmed by Eddington's 1919 solar eclipse expedition (made Einstein world-famous). Gravitational lensing is now used routinely in astronomy. (2) Gravitational time dilation: clocks in stronger gravitational fields run slower. Confirmed by the Pound-Rebka experiment (1959) using gamma rays in a tower. GPS satellites must correct for both special relativistic time dilation (satellites move fast — slows clock) and general relativistic (satellites are higher in gravitational well — speeds clock up by a larger amount). (3) Perihelion precession of Mercury: the orbit of Mercury rotates by 43 arcseconds per century more than Newtonian predictions — exactly explained by GR. (4) Gravitational waves: ripples in spacetime caused by accelerating mass — predicted by Einstein in 1916; first directly detected by LIGO in 2015 (from merging black holes 1.3 billion light-years away). (5) Black holes: regions of spacetime with curvature so extreme that even light cannot escape (Event Horizon Telescope imaged M87* and Sgr A* black holes in 2019 and 2022).
What is entropy and why does it always increase?

Entropy is a thermodynamic quantity that measures the degree of disorder or the number of microscopic configurations (microstates) corresponding to a given macroscopic state (macrostate). Boltzmann's statistical definition: S = k_B ln(W) where k_B = 1.38×10⁻²³ J/K is Boltzmann's constant and W is the number of accessible microstates. A high-entropy macrostate has many microstates (disorder); a low-entropy state has few (order). Why entropy always increases in isolated systems (Second Law): this is a statement of probability, not mechanical law. The universe tends toward higher entropy macrostates because they have vastly more corresponding microstates. For a macroscopic system with ~10²³ particles, the ratio of disordered to ordered microstates is astronomically large — the probability of spontaneous ordering (e.g., all gas molecules moving to one corner of a room) is not zero but is so vanishingly small it never observably happens. Information and entropy: Shannon entropy (information theory) is mathematically identical to thermodynamic entropy — both measure the uncertainty or information content of a system. Maxwell's Demon thought experiment: a demon that can sort fast and slow gas molecules (decreasing entropy without work) — resolution (Landauer): erasing information in the demon's memory requires energy dissipation, increasing entropy at least as much as the sorting decreases it. Arrow of time: the second law gives time its direction. The laws of mechanics are time-symmetric (they work equally well forwards and backwards); the second law breaks this symmetry — entropy increases toward the future and would have been lower in the past (low entropy initial conditions of the universe). Cosmological context: the universe began in an extremely low-entropy state (the Big Bang); the entropy has been increasing ever since; the ultimate fate is 'heat death' — maximum entropy, thermal equilibrium, no useful energy to do work.
Explain thermodynamics — the four laws and entropy.

THERMODYNAMICS — Energy, Heat, and the Laws of the Universe

ZEROTH LAW: Thermal equilibrium
"If A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in thermal equilibrium with C,
then A is in thermal equilibrium with B."
Establishes temperature as a meaningful property. Foundation for thermometers.

FIRST LAW: Conservation of Energy
"Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only converted between forms."
ΔU = Q - W
ΔU = change in internal energy
Q = heat added TO the system
W = work done BY the system

Forms of energy convert: kinetic <-> potential, thermal <-> mechanical, chemical <-> thermal.
Perpetual motion machine of the first kind is impossible (creates energy from nothing).

Examples:
 Car engine: chemical energy (fuel) -> heat -> mechanical work (shaft rotation)
 Electric motor: electrical energy -> mechanical energy
 Power plant: thermal energy -> mechanical (turbine) -> electrical

SECOND LAW: Entropy always increases
"In any spontaneous process, the total entropy of an isolated system increases."
Or: heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, not cold to hot.
Or: you cannot build a perfect heat engine (100% efficient — converts all heat to work).

ENTROPY (S): measure of disorder/number of possible microstates.
High entropy: gas spreading through room (many arrangements)
Low entropy: gas compressed into one corner (few arrangements)
The universe tends toward maximum entropy (heat death).

Why scrambled eggs can''t unscramble: the unscrambled state is astronomically improbable.
Why time seems to flow forward: entropy increases in that direction.

Efficiency of heat engine (Carnot limit):
η_max = 1 - T_cold/T_hot (temperatures in Kelvin)
If hot = 500K, cold = 300K: max efficiency = 1 - 300/500 = 40%. Can never reach 100%.

THIRD LAW: Absolute zero
"The entropy of a perfect crystal at absolute zero (0K) is zero."
Absolute zero: -273.15°C. All molecular motion ceases. Unattainable in practice.
The closer you get to 0K, the harder it gets to remove more heat.

PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS:
Refrigerator: uses work to move heat from cold (inside) to hot (outside)
 Violates "heat flows cold to hot"? No — work is input. Total entropy increases.
Heat pump: refrigerator run in reverse. Move heat from outside to inside building.
Steam turbine: hot steam -> work + cold exhaust. Limited by Carnot efficiency.
Internal combustion engine: 20-40% efficient. Most energy wasted as heat.
Explain the electromagnetic spectrum — what is light?

LIGHT is a transverse electromagnetic wave: oscillating electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to direction of travel.
Speed: 3×10^8 m/s in vacuum (c). Slows in matter: c/n (n = refractive index, n>1).

THE SPECTRUM (low frequency to high):
Radio: >1mm wavelength. AM radio, FM, WiFi, cell signals, radar.
Microwave: 1mm-30cm. Microwave oven (2.45GHz resonates water molecules). Bluetooth, WiFi.
Infrared: 700nm-1mm. Heat radiation. TV remotes, night vision, thermal cameras.
Visible: 400nm-700nm. ONLY what human eye detects.
 Red (700nm) -> Orange -> Yellow -> Green -> Blue -> Violet (400nm).
Ultraviolet: 10nm-400nm. Sunburn, vitamin D synthesis. UVA/UVB/UVC.
X-rays: 0.01nm-10nm. Medical imaging (bones absorb more than soft tissue).
Gamma rays: <0.01nm. Nuclear decay, highest energy. Penetrates everything. Deadly.

WAVE-PARTICLE DUALITY:
Light behaves as wave AND particle (photon).
Wave: diffraction, interference, polarisation.
Particle: photoelectric effect (Einstein 1905 — explains why UV ejects electrons, red light doesn''t).
E = hf (energy of photon = Planck''s constant × frequency).
Higher frequency = higher energy photon. Gamma rays most energetic.

PRACTICAL APPLICATIONS:
Visible light: vision, photography, solar panels (photovoltaic), optical fibre.
UV: sterilisation (kills bacteria by damaging DNA), fluorescence, lithography.
X-ray: medical imaging, airport security, crystallography (determine protein structures).
Microwave: cooking (dielectric heating), satellite communication.
Radio: broadcasting, GPS, radar, MRI machines (radio frequency pulses).

BLACKBODY RADIATION:
All objects emit electromagnetic radiation based on temperature.
Sun (~5778K): peaks in visible (yellow-green). Hotter = shorter wavelength.
Human body (310K): peaks in infrared (~10μm) — thermal cameras detect this.
Stefan-Boltzmann: P = σT^4. Doubling temperature: 16× power emitted.
How does quantum mechanics differ from classical physics?

QUANTUM MECHANICS — The physics of the very small (atoms, electrons, photons).

KEY DIFFERENCES FROM CLASSICAL:

1. QUANTISATION:
Classical: energy, angular momentum can be any value (continuous).
Quantum: energy comes in discrete packets (quanta).
Atom: electrons only in specific energy levels (orbits).
Photon energy: E = hf (Planck''s constant × frequency). Not continuous.

2. WAVE-PARTICLE DUALITY:
Classical: waves and particles are distinct.
Quantum: everything is both. Electrons show diffraction (wave). Photons are discrete (particle).
de Broglie wavelength: λ = h/mv. Even baseballs have a wavelength (too small to observe).

3. UNCERTAINTY PRINCIPLE (Heisenberg):
Classical: can precisely know position AND momentum simultaneously.
Quantum: ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2. More precisely you know position, less you know momentum.
Not a measurement problem — a fundamental property of nature.
ΔEΔt ≥ ℏ/2: can''t know exact energy for arbitrarily short time. Virtual particles possible.

4. SUPERPOSITION:
Classical: object is here OR there.
Quantum: particle can be in multiple states simultaneously until measured.
Schrödinger''s cat: superposition of alive and dead until observed.
Wavefunction ψ: describes probability amplitudes for all possible states.
Measurement collapses wavefunction to one outcome.

5. ENTANGLEMENT:
Two particles can be "entangled" — measuring one instantly affects the other, regardless of distance.
Not faster-than-light communication (can''t control which result you get).
"Spooky action at a distance" (Einstein). Proven real by Bell test experiments (2022 Nobel Prize).

WHERE CLASSICAL WORKS:
Large objects, everyday speeds. Classical mechanics emerges from quantum for large systems.
Correspondence principle: quantum results approach classical for large quantum numbers.

QUANTUM APPLICATIONS:
Transistors (computers), lasers, MRI machines, atomic clocks (GPS), solar cells.
Quantum computing: harness superposition and entanglement for certain computations.
Explain optics — lenses, refraction, and how cameras work.

OPTICS — The Study of Light Behaviour

REFRACTION:
Light bends when passing between materials of different optical density (refractive index).
Snell''s Law: n₁sinθ₁ = n₂sinθ₂
Air (n=1.0) to glass (n=1.5): light bends toward normal (slower in glass).
Glass to air: bends away from normal.

Total internal reflection: if angle too steep when going from dense to less dense medium -> no transmission.
Used in: optical fibres (light trapped inside fibre by TIR), diamond (high n creates sparkle).

LENSES:
Convex (converging): thicker in middle. Converges parallel rays to focal point.
Concave (diverging): thinner in middle. Diverges parallel rays (appear to come from focal point).

Thin lens equation: 1/f = 1/do + 1/di
f = focal length, do = object distance, di = image distance.

Magnification: m = -di/do. Negative = inverted image.

Real image: rays actually converge. Can be projected on screen. Inverted.
Virtual image: rays appear to diverge from point. Cannot project. Upright. Mirror/magnifying glass.

HOW A CAMERA WORKS:
1. Lens system focuses light onto sensor (or film).
2. Aperture (iris): controls amount of light. Wider = more light, shallower depth of field.
3. Shutter: controls duration of exposure. Faster = less motion blur, needs more light.
4. Sensor (CMOS/CCD): converts photon intensity to electrical signal per pixel.
5. Pixel values recorded as image file.

Depth of field: range of distances that appear sharp.
Large aperture (f/1.8): shallow DOF. Small aperture (f/16): deep DOF.

THE EYE:
Cornea + lens: adjustable lens system (accommodation) focuses image on retina.
Retina: contains rods (low light, no colour) and cones (colour: red, green, blue).
Fovea: highest cone density. Central vision. Peripheral: mostly rods.
Optic nerve blind spot: no photoreceptors where nerve exits. Brain fills in.
Explain electricity and circuits — Ohm''s Law, series, and parallel.

ELECTRICITY — Fundamentals

BASIC CONCEPTS:
Charge (Q): measured in coulombs. Electrons carry negative charge.
Current (I): flow of charge per second. Amperes (A). I = Q/t.
Voltage (V): electrical potential difference. Volts (V). Energy per unit charge.
Resistance (R): opposition to current flow. Ohms (Ω).
Power (P): rate of energy use. Watts (W).

OHM''S LAW: V = IR
Current through resistor = voltage across it divided by resistance.
I = V/R. R = V/I.

POWER: P = IV = I²R = V²/R.
 1000W electric kettle at 230V: I = P/V = 1000/230 = 4.35A.

SERIES CIRCUITS:
Components connected end-to-end. Same current through all.
Total resistance: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + R₃.
Voltage divides: V across each = I × R (proportional to resistance).
3Ω + 2Ω = 5Ω total. If V=10V: I=2A. V₁=6V, V₂=4V.

PARALLEL CIRCUITS:
Components connected across same two nodes. Same voltage across all.
Total resistance: 1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + 1/R₃.
Current divides: I through each = V/R (inversely proportional to resistance).
3Ω parallel 2Ω: 1/R = 1/3+1/2 = 5/6. R=1.2Ω. Less than either! More paths = less resistance.

Home wiring: always parallel. All appliances get full 230V.
Series problem: if one fails, all fail. Christmas lights (old type).

KIRCHHOFF''S LAWS:
KCL (Current Law): sum of currents entering node = sum leaving. Charge conserved.
KVL (Voltage Law): sum of voltages around any closed loop = 0. Energy conserved.

CAPACITORS: store charge. C = Q/V. Farads (F). Block DC, pass AC.
INDUCTORS: store energy in magnetic field. H (Henry). Resist change in current.
DIODES: allow current in one direction only. Rectification (AC -> DC).
TRANSISTORS: amplify or switch current. Basis of all digital logic.
How does nuclear fission and fusion work?

NUCLEAR REACTIONS — energy from atomic nuclei

NUCLEAR FISSION:
Heavy nucleus splits into smaller fragments + neutrons + energy.
U-235 + neutron -> Kr-92 + Ba-141 + 3 neutrons + ~200 MeV energy.

Why energy released? Binding energy per nucleon is higher for mid-size nuclei.
Mass-energy: E = mc². Tiny mass difference (mass defect) = enormous energy.
200 MeV per fission vs ~4 eV per chemical reaction. Million times more energy per atom.

CHAIN REACTION:
3 neutrons released -> can each trigger more fissions -> exponential increase.
Critical mass: enough U-235 that neutrons are more likely to hit another nucleus than escape.
Control rods (boron, hafnium): absorb neutrons to control reaction rate.
Moderator (water, graphite): slow neutrons (thermal neutrons more likely to cause fission).

NUCLEAR POWER:
Controlled chain reaction heats water -> steam -> turbine -> electricity.
No CO2 emissions during operation. Energy density: 1kg U-235 = ~1500 tonnes of coal.
Issues: radioactive waste, proliferation risk, public perception, high upfront cost.

NUCLEAR FUSION:
Small nuclei merge to form larger nucleus + energy.
D + T -> He-4 + neutron + 17.6 MeV.
Why energy? Products have less total mass (converted to energy).

Fusion of hydrogen: what powers stars (including Sun).
Sun: proton-proton chain reaction. Core: 15 million K, enormous pressure.
Conditions on Earth: need plasma at 100+ million K (hotter than sun core due to less pressure).

FUSION ADVANTAGES over fission:
Fuel: deuterium from seawater (nearly unlimited). Tritium from lithium.
No long-lived radioactive waste (products: helium, tritium manageable).
No chain reaction: inherently safe — stop heating = reaction stops.

STATUS: ITER (France) and private companies (Commonwealth Fusion, TAE Technologies) working on it.
"Fusion is always 30 years away" — may be changing. NIF achieved ignition (2022).
